passages.original: quam ob rem quoniam ab hac laude proficisceris et quicquid es ex hoc es, ita paratus ad dicendum venito quasi in singulis causis iudicium de omni ingenio futurum sit. eius facultatis adiumenta, quae tibi scio esse seposita, ut parata ac prompta sint cura et saepe quae de Demosthenis studio et exercitatione scripsit Demetrius recordare, deinde ut amicorum et multitudo et genera appareant. habes enim ea quae non multi homines novi habuerunt, omnis publicanos, totum fere equestrem ordinem, multa propria municipia, multos abs te defensos homines cuiusque ordinis, aliquot collegia, praeterea studio dicendi conciliatos plurimos adulescentulos, cotidianam amicorum assiduitatem et frequentiam.
passages.english: Therefore, since you set out from this distinction, and whatever you are, you are because of it, come prepared for speaking as if in each individual case a verdict were going to be passed on your whole talent. See to it that the resources of that faculty, which I know you have stored away, are ready and at hand, and often recall what Demetrius wrote about the study and practice of Demosthenes; then see to it that both the number and the variety of your friends are evident. For you have what not many new men have had: all the tax-farmers, almost the whole equestrian order, many towns attached to you, many men of every order defended by you, a number of associations, and besides these a great many young men won over by their enthusiasm for oratory, [and] the daily attendance and crowds of your friends.
passages.notes: "Demetrius" is presumably Demetrius of Phalerum. The syntax of "eius facultatis adiumenta ... ut parata ac prompta sint cura" is compressed: "cura ut" governs both this clause and the later "deinde ut ... appareant". "Collegia" may mean guilds or religious associations. "Municipia" are Italian towns, here ones with a special tie to the candidate.
